items.title: RBI — Establishment, Structure & Functions
items.body:
## In one line

The **Reserve Bank of India** is India's central bank — it issues currency, sets monetary policy and regulates banks. It is asked because APPSC Prelims regularly tests its founding year, legal basis and core functions.

## Establishment

- The **Reserve Bank of India Act was passed in 1934**; the RBI **began operations on 1 April 1935**, and was **nationalised on 1 January 1949**.
- Headquartered in **Mumbai**; the current Governor (Sep 2026) is **Sanjay Malhotra**.

## Organisational structure

- Its affairs are governed by a **Central Board of Directors** appointed by the Government of India; directors serve a fixed **four-year term**.
- The Board comprises a **Governor and not more than four Deputy Governors** (the full-time officials); plus 10 government-nominated directors and 4 from local boards (Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Delhi).

## Core functions

| Function | What it means |
|---|---|
| Monetary authority | Frames and implements monetary policy for price stability + growth; its main instrument is the **repo rate** |
| Sole issuer of currency | The sole authority for issuing currency notes ≥ ₹2; coins and the ₹1 note are issued by the Government of India (the ₹1 note carries the Finance Secretary's signature, not the Governor's) |
| Banker's bank | Holds banks' reserves, settles claims; as **lender of last resort** it is the banker's bank providing emergency funds to banks in distress |
| Banker to government | Manages accounts and **public debt** (G-secs) |
| Custodian of forex | Manages reserves and the rupee under **FEMA (1999)** |
| Regulator & supervisor | Oversees commercial/cooperative banks and regulates **NBFCs** under the **RBI Act & prudential norms** |
| Developmental role | Financial inclusion, digital payments (UPI, BBPS) |

## Terms explained

- **Statutory body** — a body created by an Act of Parliament (the RBI Act, 1934), not by the Constitution.
- **Nationalisation** — transfer of ownership from private hands to the government (RBI, 1 Jan 1949).
- **Lender of last resort** — the RBI gives emergency funds to a bank in crisis when no one else will.
- **G-secs** — government securities (bonds the government issues to borrow).

## TL;DR

- RBI Act passed 1934; RBI began operations 1 April 1935; nationalised 1 January 1949; HQ Mumbai.
- Central Board appointed by GoI for a four-year term; Governor + up to four Deputy Governors.
- RBI is the sole issuer of currency notes; coins and the ₹1 note are issued by the Government of India.
- As banker's bank it is the lender of last resort; as banker to government it manages public debt.
- Forex reserves are managed under FEMA 1999; RBI also regulates banks and NBFCs.
keyPoints: RBI Act passed 1934; RBI began operations 1 April 1935; nationalised 1 January 1949; HQ Mumbai.
Central Board appointed by GoI for a four-year term; Governor + up to four Deputy Governors.
RBI is the sole issuer of currency notes; coins and the ₹1 note are issued by the Government of India.
As banker's bank it is the lender of last resort; as banker to government it manages public debt.
Forex reserves are managed under FEMA 1999; RBI also regulates banks and NBFCs.
Current RBI Governor (Sep 2026): Sanjay Malhotra.

items.title: Monetary Policy Tools & the LAF Corridor
items.body:
## In one line

**Monetary policy tools** are the levers the RBI uses to control how much money and credit flow in the economy. Examiners love the repo/CRR/SLR definitions and the current policy-rate values.

## Quantitative (general) tools

- **Repo rate** — rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks against G-secs; introduced under the **LAF in 2000**. Raise → curb inflation; cut → spur growth.
- **Reverse repo / SDF** — the **Standing Deposit Facility (2022)** replaced the fixed reverse repo as the LAF **floor**; lets banks park surplus funds with the RBI **without collateral**.
- **MSF — Marginal Standing Facility (2011)** — banks borrow at a **penal rate** set higher than the repo rate (LAF ceiling); the **Bank Rate** is currently aligned with the MSF rate.
- **CRR** — a percentage of deposits kept as cash reserves **with the RBI** (earns no interest).
- **SLR** — maintained in liquid assets like cash, gold and G-secs, held by the **bank itself**.
- **OMO (1992)** — buy G-secs = inject liquidity; sell = absorb. **MSS (2004)** sterilises capital inflows.
- **Absorbing excess liquidity from large capital inflows:** the RBI would be selling government securities through **OMO** and issuing securities under the **MSS** (Market Stabilisation Scheme). Cutting CRR/repo or buying G-secs would do the opposite (inject money).

## Policy rates — as of October 2026

The repo rate was raised by 25 bps to 5.50% at the 7 October 2026 MPC meeting; the RBI Governor is **Sanjay Malhotra** (since December 2024).

| Rate | Value |
|---|---|
| Policy repo rate | **5.50%** |
| SDF (corridor floor) | 5.25% |
| MSF / Bank Rate (ceiling) | 5.75% |
| CRR | 3.00% |
| SLR | 18.00% |

The LAF corridor is symmetric: **SDF (repo − 0.25) < repo < MSF (repo + 0.25)**.

## Terms explained

- **LAF** — Liquidity Adjustment Facility: the window (since 2000) through which the RBI lends (repo) or absorbs (SDF) money overnight.
- **Repo rate** — the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against G-secs.
- **CRR** — Cash Reserve Ratio: cash banks must keep with the RBI (no interest).
- **SLR** — Statutory Liquidity Ratio: liquid assets (cash/gold/G-secs) a bank keeps with itself.
- **Sterilisation** — mopping up extra money from foreign inflows (via OMO sales / MSS).

## TL;DR

- Repo rate introduced under the LAF in 2000; OMO began 1992; MSS 2004; MSF 2011.
- SDF (2022) is the LAF floor and absorbs liquidity without collateral; MSF is the penal ceiling.
- CRR is cash held with the RBI (no interest); SLR is liquid assets held by the bank itself.
- As of Oct 2026: repo 5.50%, SDF 5.25%, MSF/Bank Rate 5.75%, CRR 3.00%, SLR 18.00%.
- OMO buy/MSS absorb-issue are used to inject or drain systemic liquidity.

SDF (2022) is the LAF floor and absorbs liquidity without collateral; MSF is the penal ceiling.

Corridor is symmetric around the repo rate (±0.25%).

items.title: MPC & Inflation Targeting
items.body:
## In one line

The **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)** is the six-member body that fixes the repo rate to keep inflation near a 4% target. It is asked for its composition, voting and the inflation band.

## Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)

- Established in **2016** via an amendment to the **RBI Act, 1934** (Section 45ZB), shifting from a Governor-centric to a committee model.
- **Six members** = 3 RBI (Governor as Chair + Deputy Governor for monetary policy + one RBI officer) and **3 external experts** appointed by the GoI.
- Meets **at least 4 times a year** (about once every two months); **quorum 4**; each member one vote; the **Governor has a casting vote** in a tie.

## Flexible inflation targeting

- India targets **CPI inflation of 4% with a ±2% tolerance band (2%–6%)**.
- The target is set by the Government in consultation with the RBI and **reviewed every five years**.
- CPI is compiled by the **National Statistical Office (NSO)**.

## Terms explained

- **MPC** — Monetary Policy Committee: the six-member panel that votes on the repo rate.
- **Casting vote** — the extra vote the Governor uses to break a 3–3 tie.
- **Flexible inflation targeting** — a legal promise to keep CPI inflation at 4%, allowing a 2%–6% band.
- **CPI** — Consumer Price Index: measures retail price rise, compiled by the NSO.

## TL;DR

- MPC established 2016 under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act, 1934.
- Six members: 3 from RBI (Governor chairs) + 3 government-appointed external experts.
- MPC meets at least four times a year; quorum four; Governor holds the casting vote.
- Inflation target: 4% CPI with a ±2% band (2%–6%), reviewed every five years.
- CPI (the target measure) is compiled by the NSO.

items.title: Money Supply & the Money Multiplier
items.body:
## In one line

**Money supply** is the total money circulating in the economy (measured as M0–M4), and the **money multiplier** shows how a small base of reserve money expands into much larger bank deposits. Asked for aggregate definitions and a simple multiplier sum.

## Monetary aggregates (RBI classification)

| Aggregate | Composition |
|---|---|
| **M0** (reserve / high-powered money) | Currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI |
| **M1** (narrow money) | Currency with public + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI |
| **M2** | M1 + savings deposits with post-office savings banks |
| **M3** (broad money) | M1 + time deposits with banks |
| **M4** | M3 + total post-office deposits |

- Liquidity decreases from M1 → M4; **M3** is the most-watched 'broad money'.

## Money multiplier

- **Money multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio** (simple case). Example: RR 20% → multiplier = 1/0.20 = **5**.
- It captures how a small rise in reserve money (M0) expands total deposits through lending and re-deposit.
- Inverse relationship with the reserve ratio; a higher **currency-to-deposit ratio** or cash leakage lowers it.

## Terms explained

- **M0 (reserve/high-powered money)** — currency plus banks' deposits with the RBI.
- **M3 (broad money)** — M1 plus time (fixed) deposits; the most-watched measure.
- **Reserve ratio** — the share of deposits a bank must hold back (CRR + SLR).
- **Money multiplier** — how many rupees of deposits each rupee of reserve money creates (= 1 ÷ reserve ratio).

## TL;DR

- M0 = high-powered/reserve money; M1 = narrow money; M3 = broad money (M1 + time deposits).
- Liquidity falls from M1 to M4; M3 is the key 'broad money' aggregate.
- Money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio; RR 20% gives a multiplier of 5.
- The multiplier has an inverse relationship with the reserve ratio.
- A higher currency-to-deposit ratio or cash leakage reduces the actual multiplier.
keyPoints: M0 = high-powered/reserve money; M1 = narrow money; M3 = broad money (M1 + time deposits).
Liquidity falls from M1 to M4; M3 is the key 'broad money' aggregate.
Money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio; RR 20% gives a multiplier of 5.
The multiplier has an inverse relationship with the reserve ratio.
A higher currency-to-deposit ratio or cash leakage reduces the actual multiplier.
items.mnemonic: Broad-to-narrow: M1 is 'lively' (liquid), M3 adds time deposits, M4 adds all post-office money.

items.title: Banking Structure, Nationalisation & NPA Management
items.body:
## In one line

This note explains how India's **banks are classified**, the history of **nationalisation/merger**, and the tools used to recover **bad loans (NPAs)**. Asked for bank types, the 1969/1980/2020 milestones and SARFAESI/IBC.

## Classification of banks

- **Scheduled banks** are those included (listed) in the **Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934** and can borrow from the RBI; **non-scheduled banks** are not.
- **Scheduled commercial banks**: public sector, private sector, foreign, **Regional Rural Banks (RRBs)**, and **small finance banks**.
- Newer categories: **Small Finance Banks** (financial inclusion) and **Payments Banks** (deposits + payments, but **cannot lend or issue credit cards**).

## Nationalisation & consolidation

| Event | Year | Number |
|---|---|---|
| First nationalisation | 1969 | 14 major private banks nationalised |
| Second round of nationalisation | 1980 | 6 more banks nationalised |
| Mega-merger | 2020 | Ten public-sector banks merged into four |

## Managing NPAs

- **SARFAESI Act, 2002** — recover secured loans without court intervention.
- **IBC, 2016** — time-bound insolvency resolution via the NCLT.
- **Prompt Corrective Action (PCA)** — RBI curbs on weak banks (capital/asset-quality triggers).
- **Priority-Sector Lending** — directed credit: 40% of adjusted net bank credit to agriculture, MSMEs, weaker sections.

## Terms explained

- **Scheduled bank** — a bank listed in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934.
- **NPA (non-performing asset)** — a loan on which repayment is overdue beyond 90 days.
- **SARFAESI (2002)** — lets banks seize and sell a defaulter's secured assets without going to court.
- **IBC (2016)** — Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code: time-bound resolution of defaults via the NCLT.
- **PCA** — Prompt Corrective Action: RBI curbs on a weak bank.

## TL;DR

- Scheduled banks are in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934; RRBs are scheduled commercial banks.
- Payments banks take deposits and offer payments but cannot lend or issue credit cards.
- Bank nationalisation: 14 banks in 1969, 6 in 1980; 2020 mega-merger cut 10 PSBs to 4.
- SARFAESI 2002 enables recovery of secured loans without courts; IBC 2016 gives time-bound insolvency.
- PCA imposes RBI restrictions on weak banks; PSL target is 40% of adjusted net bank credit.

items.title: Financial Markets, Inflation & Other Regulators
items.body:
## In one line

This note covers India's **financial markets**, the **types of inflation** and the **non-banking regulators** (SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA). Asked for money-vs-capital market, core-vs-headline inflation and which body regulates what.

## Financial markets

- **Money market** — deals with short-term instruments maturing in one year or less: T-bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit, call money.
- **Capital market** — long-term equity and debt; split into **primary** (new issues/IPOs) and **secondary** (trading on NSE/BSE).
- **SEBI** (established in **1992**) regulates the securities market; **RBI** oversees the money market; the **FSDC** coordinates across regulators.
- **Lending-rate benchmarks:** the **MCLR (Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate)** was introduced by the RBI in **2016**, replacing the earlier base-rate system. Its principal objective is greater transparency and faster transmission of policy-rate changes to borrowers. New floating-rate retail and MSME loans are now linked instead to an **external benchmark (EBLR, such as the repo rate)**.

## Inflation — types & measures

- **Demand-pull** ('too much money chasing too few goods') vs **cost-push** (arises from rising input costs) vs **structural** inflation.
- **Headline CPI** includes all items; **core inflation** excludes volatile food and fuel.
- Measures: **CPI** (compiled by NSO), **WPI** (Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT), GDP deflator, PPI.
- The **Phillips curve** shows the short-run inverse inflation–unemployment trade-off.

## Other regulators & inclusion

- **IRDAI (Act 1999)** — insurance-sector regulator; **PFRDA** — pension-sector regulator overseeing the **NPS** and **Atal Pension Yojana (APY)**, which gives a guaranteed minimum pension for the unorganised sector.
- **PM Jan Dhan Yojana (2014)** — financial inclusion through zero-balance bank accounts; it anchored the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) for direct benefit transfer.

## Terms explained

- **Money market** — market for short-term funds (one year or less).
- **Capital market** — market for long-term equity and debt.
- **Primary vs secondary market** — new issues (IPOs) vs trading of existing securities.
- **Core inflation** — the price trend after removing volatile food and fuel.
- **SEBI / IRDAI / PFRDA** — regulators of securities / insurance / pensions.

## TL;DR

- Money market = short-term (≤1 yr) instruments; capital market = long-term equity/debt.
- MCLR (2016) is the transparency-focused lending benchmark that replaced the base rate; new loans use an external benchmark (EBLR).
- Primary market issues new securities (IPOs); secondary market trades existing ones on NSE/BSE.
- SEBI (1992) regulates securities; CPI is compiled by NSO, WPI by the Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT).
- Core inflation excludes food and fuel; headline CPI includes all items.

items.title: Digital Payments — NPCI, UPI & the Digital Rupee
items.body:
## In one line

This note explains India's **digital-payments system** — the NPCI, UPI, card/transfer networks and the Digital Rupee. Asked heavily as current affairs: who runs UPI, latest volumes and the CBDC pilots.

## NPCI & its products

- **NPCI** (set up in 2008) is the not-for-profit umbrella organisation for retail payments, promoted by the **RBI and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA)** under the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**.
- Flagship products: **RuPay** (domestic card network, 2012), **IMPS** (2010), **UPI** (2016) and **Bharat BillPay/BBPS** (an interoperable platform for recurring bill payments).

## Fund-transfer systems

| System | Operator | Feature |
|---|---|---|
| RTGS | RBI | Real-time gross settlement for large value (≥₹2 lakh), operated by the RBI; 24x7 since Dec 2020 |
| NEFT | RBI | Retail transfer settled by the RBI in batches, with no minimum amount; 24x7 since Dec 2019 |
| IMPS | NPCI | 24x7 instant mobile transfer (2010) |
| UPI | NPCI | Instant VPA-based P2P/P2M (2016), interoperable |

## UPI — scale (verified Sep 2026)

- Launched by NPCI in 2016; **completed ten years of operation in August 2026**.
- **August 2025:** UPI processed about **20 billion transactions** worth roughly **₹25 lakh crore** in a single month.
- **FY 2025-26 value ≈ ₹314 lakh crore**; India ≈ half of the world's real-time digital payments.
- From **14 September 2026**, banks and payment providers are barred from levying charges on UPI transactions up to ₹2,000 (and on RuPay debit cards).

## Newer instruments

- **e-RUPI** (2021) — a prepaid, person- and purpose-specific digital voucher delivered as a QR code or SMS; needs no bank account or app at the beneficiary's end.
- **Digital Rupee (e₹, CBDC)** — RBI's sovereign digital currency and legal tender issued by the RBI, unlike privately issued cryptocurrencies; **wholesale pilot 1 Nov 2022**, **retail pilot 1 Dec 2022**.
- **UPI global** — linked with Singapore's **PayNow (2023)** to enable cross-border remittances; India and France have enabled UPI acceptance for Indian users abroad (UPI is also accepted in UAE, France, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Mauritius — via NPCI International Payments Ltd).
- **Payments banks** — introduced on the recommendation of the **Nachiket Mor Committee**, RBI guidelines 2014; may accept deposits up to **₹2 lakh per customer** but cannot lend or issue credit cards. Examples: **India Post Payments Bank, Airtel Payments Bank**.

## Terms explained

- **NPCI** — National Payments Corporation of India: the not-for-profit umbrella that runs retail payments.
- **UPI** — Unified Payments Interface: instant bank-to-bank payment using a virtual address.
- **VPA** — Virtual Payment Address, e.g. name@bank, used instead of account numbers.
- **CBDC / Digital Rupee (e₹)** — digital cash issued by the RBI; it is legal tender.
- **e-RUPI** — a prepaid, purpose-specific e-voucher sent as a QR code or SMS.

## TL;DR

- NPCI (2008), promoted by RBI & IBA under the PSS Act 2007, runs RuPay (2012), IMPS (2010), UPI (2016) and BBPS.
- RTGS (≥₹2 lakh) and NEFT are RBI systems, both now 24x7; IMPS and UPI are NPCI systems.
- UPI launched 2016, completed 10 years in Aug 2026; Aug 2025 saw ~20 billion transactions worth ~₹25 lakh crore.
- UPI value reached ~₹314 lakh crore in FY 2025-26; from 14 Sep 2026 no charges on UPI up to ₹2,000.
- e-RUPI (2021) is a prepaid purpose-specific voucher needing no account/app at the recipient's end.

items.title: RBI History, Governors & PYQ Precision on RBI Powers
items.body:
**In one line:** the RBI was proposed by the Hilton Young Commission, began in Calcutta in 1935, moved to Bombay, was nationalised in 1949, and is now led by its 26th Governor, Sanjay Malhotra.

**Why it is asked:** RBI firsts and UPSC 2021/2025 questions on the Governor's appointment and RBI's income are standard.

## Timeline

**The story**

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| **1926** | **Hilton Young Commission** (Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance) recommends a central bank |
| **1934** | **RBI Act** passed |
| **1 April 1935** | RBI starts in **Calcutta** as a shareholders' bank |
| **1937** | Head office moves permanently to **Bombay** |
| **1 January 1949** | RBI **nationalised** |
| **1949** | **Banking Regulation Act** — RBI's power to license and supervise banks |

## Governors

- **First Governor:** **Sir Osborne Smith**; **first Indian Governor:** **C.D. Deshmukh**.
- **Sanjay Malhotra** became the **26th Governor** on **11 December 2024**, succeeding Shaktikanta Das (the source text still names Das).
- Up to **four Deputy Governors** (e.g. **Poonam Gupta**, in charge of monetary policy).

## PYQ precision

- **UPSC 2021:** the Governor is **appointed by the Central Government**, and draws his powers from the **RBI Act, 1934** — the Constitution does **not** give the Centre power to direct the RBI.
- **UPSC 2021:** as **lender of last resort** the RBI provides liquidity to banks in a temporary crisis.
- **UPSC 2025:** the RBI earns income from **buying and selling government bonds** and **buying and selling foreign currency** — not from printing currency, pension funds or lending to private companies.

## Other functions (source)

- **Issuer of currency** (coins by the Government), **banker to the government** (Centre and States), **banker's bank**, custodian of **forex reserves** under **FEMA**, regulator of banks and **NBFCs**, and promoter of **UPI** and **Bharat Bill Payment System (BBPS)**.

**Don't confuse** — *Hilton Young Commission* (1926, recommended RBI) with the *RBI Act* (1934) and the *start of operations* (1935).

**TL;DR**
- Hilton Young 1926 → RBI Act 1934 → 1 April 1935 Calcutta → Bombay 1937 → nationalised 1 Jan 1949; BR Act 1949.
- First Governor Osborne Smith; first Indian C.D. Deshmukh; Sanjay Malhotra 26th (11 Dec 2024).
- Governor appointed by Centre, powers from RBI Act; RBI income = G-bond and forex operations.
keyPoints: The Hilton Young Commission (1926) recommended a central bank for India.
RBI began on 1 April 1935 in Calcutta; its head office moved permanently to Bombay in 1937.
RBI was nationalised on 1 January 1949; the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 empowers it to regulate banks.
First RBI Governor: Sir Osborne Smith; first Indian Governor: C.D. Deshmukh.
Sanjay Malhotra became the 26th RBI Governor on 11 December 2024, succeeding Shaktikanta Das.
Poonam Gupta is the Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy.
The RBI Governor is appointed by the Central Government and draws powers from the RBI Act, 1934 (UPSC 2021).
As lender of last resort the RBI provides liquidity to banks in a temporary crisis (UPSC 2021).
RBI earns income from buying and selling government bonds and foreign currency (UPSC 2025).
RBI promotes UPI and the Bharat Bill Payment System (BBPS).

items.title: The 2025-26 Rate Cycle, Policy-Tool PYQs, Inflation Types & Price Indices
items.body:
**In one line:** the RBI cut the repo rate from 6.50% to 5.25% during 2025, then on 7 October 2026 raised it to 5.50% as inflation neared 6%; inflation is measured by a rebased CPI (2024) and WPI (2022-23).

**Why it is asked:** current policy rates, the direction of each tool (UPSC 2013-2023) and index facts are high-frequency.

## The rate cycle

**The story**

| Date | Repo rate |
|---|---|
| Feb 2023 – Dec 2024 | **6.50%** held for **11** meetings |
| Feb – Jun 2025 | Cut to 6.25%, 6.00%, then **5.50%** (a 50 bps cut in June 2025) |
| **December 2025** | **5.25%** — total easing **125 bps** |
| **7 October 2026** | Raised **25 bps to 5.50%**; stance changed from neutral to **"calibrated tightening"** |

- After the hike: **SDF 5.25%**, **MSF and Bank Rate 5.75%**; **CRR 3%** (cut by 100 bps in phases from June 2025, releasing about **₹2.5 lakh crore**); **SLR 18%**.
- The RBI raised its 2026-27 inflation projection to **5.2%** and growth to **7.1%**. CPI inflation was **5.54%** in **September 2026**; forex reserves were about **$726 billion** (9 Oct 2026).
- In March 2026 the Government retained the **4% (±2%) CPI target until March 2031**.

## Tool-direction PYQs

| Action | Meaning (UPSC) |
|---|---|
| Raising the **Bank Rate** | **Tight money** policy (2013) |
| **OMO** | Purchase and sale of **government securities** (2013) |
| **Sterilisation** | Done through **OMOs** (2023) |
| Cutting **SLR** | Banks may **cut lending rates** (2015) |
| Expansionary policy | RBI would **not raise the MSF rate** (2020) |
| Components of monetary policy | **Bank rate and OMO** — not public debt or revenue (2015) |
| "MSF rate" and "NDTL" | Terms of **banking operations** (2014) |

## Inflation types (source)

| Type | Rate |
|---|---|
| **Creeping** | about **1-5%** a year |
| **Trotting** (walking) | **5-10%** |
| **Galloping** | **10-20%** |
| **Hyperinflation** | over **50% a month** (Weimar Germany, Zimbabwe 2007-08) |

- **Demand-pull** = "too much money chasing too few goods"; **cost-push** = supply shocks such as oil; **structural** = backward farming and poor distribution.
- India's inflation peaked at **28.6% in 1974**.
- **Quantity theory:** **MV = PQ** — **Milton Friedman** and the monetarists; **Keynes** warned of a **liquidity trap**.

## Price indices

| Index | Compiler | Base |
|---|---|---|
| **CPI** | **NSO** | **2024** (new series from early 2026; **358** items, up from 299; old base 2012) |
| **WPI** | **Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT** | **2022-23** from **15 June 2026** (old 2011-12), alongside a new **Producer Price Index** |
| **CPI-IW** | **Labour Bureau** | — |
| **GDP deflator** | NSO | covers the whole economy |

- **WPI** excludes **services**; manufactured goods carry the highest WPI weight. In the CPI, **food** carries the highest weight.

**Don't confuse** — *SDF* (5.25%, floor, no collateral) with *MSF* (5.75%, ceiling, penal); and *CPI* (NSO, target index) with *WPI* (DPIIT, no services).

**TL;DR**
- 6.50% (11 meetings) → cuts to 5.25% (Dec 2025, 125 bps) → hike to 5.50% (7 Oct 2026, "calibrated tightening").
- SDF 5.25, MSF/Bank Rate 5.75, CRR 3 (from June 2025), SLR 18; CPI Sept 2026 5.54%; target 4% ±2% to Mar 2031.
- Bank rate up = tight money; OMO = G-sec trade; sterilisation via OMO; SLR cut → lower lending rates.
- Creeping 1-5, trotting 5-10, galloping 10-20, hyper >50%/month; 1974 peak 28.6%; MV = PQ.
- CPI base 2024 (358 items, NSO); WPI base 2022-23 (OEA, DPIIT) + PPI from 15 June 2026.
keyPoints: The repo rate was held at 6.50% for 11 meetings (Feb 2023 – Dec 2024).
In 2025 the RBI cut the repo rate by 125 bps in phases, including a 50 bps cut in June 2025, to 5.25% in December 2025.
On 7 October 2026 the MPC raised the repo rate by 25 bps to 5.50% and changed its stance from neutral to 'calibrated tightening'.
After the October 2026 hike: SDF 5.25%, MSF and Bank Rate 5.75%; CRR 3% (cut 100 bps from June 2025, about ₹2.5 lakh crore released); SLR 18%.
RBI projected 2026-27 inflation at 5.2% and growth at 7.1%; CPI inflation was 5.54% in September 2026; forex reserves about $726 billion.
In March 2026 the Government retained the 4% (±2%) CPI inflation target until March 2031.
The MPC decides the RBI's benchmark interest rates; it is chaired by the RBI Governor, not the Finance Minister, and has six members, not twelve (UPSC 2017).
A rise in the Bank Rate indicates tight money policy; OMO means purchase and sale of government securities (UPSC 2013).
Sterilisation is done through Open Market Operations (UPSC 2023).
A cut in SLR lets scheduled commercial banks cut lending rates; Bank rate and OMO are components of monetary policy, while public debt and public revenue are not (UPSC 2015).
In an expansionary policy the RBI would not increase the Marginal Standing Facility rate (UPSC 2020); MSF and NDTL are banking-operations terms (UPSC 2014).
Inflation types (source): creeping 1-5%, trotting 5-10%, galloping 10-20%, hyperinflation over 50% a month.
Demand-pull inflation is 'too much money chasing too few goods'; structural inflation stems from backward agriculture and poor distribution.
India's inflation peaked at 28.6% in 1974.
Quantity theory MV = PQ is linked to Milton Friedman and the monetarists; Keynes warned of a liquidity trap.
CPI is compiled by the NSO (Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation) with base 2024 (358 items, up from 299; old base 2012).
WPI (Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT) moved to base 2022-23 from 15 June 2026, alongside a new Producer Price Index.
CPI-IW is compiled by the Labour Bureau; WPI excludes services; food has the highest CPI weight.

items.title: Banking History, Nationalisation, Committees, RRBs & 2025-26 Banking Changes
items.body:
**In one line:** Indian banking ran from the Bank of Hindustan (1770) through two nationalisations and the Narasimham reforms to today's 12 PSBs, 28 RRBs and a four-nominee rule.

**Why it is asked:** firsts, nationalisation dates, committee-to-reform pairs, Basel/PSL numbers and AP's Andhra Bank are recurring.

## Firsts and early history

**The story**

| Bank | Year |
|---|---|
| **Bank of Hindustan** — first bank (Calcutta) | **1770** |
| **General Bank of India** | **1786** |
| **Presidency Banks** (Bengal, Bombay, Madras) | 1806-1843 → merged into the **Imperial Bank of India (1921)** → **State Bank of India (1 July 1955)** |
| **Punjab National Bank** — first bank wholly managed by Indians | **1894** (Lahore) |
| **Andhra Bank** — founded by **Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya** at **Machilipatnam** | **1923**; merged into **Union Bank of India** on **1 April 2020** |

## Nationalisation and consolidation

- **19 July 1969:** **14** banks (deposits above ₹50 crore) nationalised; **15 April 1980:** **6** more (deposits above ₹200 crore).
- **1 April 2019:** Dena Bank and Vijaya Bank merged into **Bank of Baroda**; **1 April 2020:** 10 PSBs merged into 4 — leaving **12 public sector banks**.

## Committees

| Committee | Year | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| **Narasimham I** | **1991** | Cut SLR/CRR, prudential norms, entry of private banks |
| **Narasimham II** | **1998** | Bank mergers, ARCs, capital adequacy |
| **Raghuram Rajan** (financial sector reforms) | **2008** | "Hundred small steps" |
| **Nachiket Mor** | **2013** | **Payments banks** and **small finance banks** (licensed 2014-15) |
| **P.J. Nayak** | **2014** | Bank governance → **Banks Board Bureau (2016)**, now **FSIB (2022)** |
| **Urjit Patel** | **2014** | **Flexible inflation targeting** (CPI) |

## Regional Rural Banks

- First RRB: **Prathama Bank**, Moradabad, **2 October 1975**; **RRB Act, 1976**; shareholding **Centre 50 : Sponsor bank 35 : State 15**.
- **One State, One RRB** (from **1 May 2025**) cut RRBs from **43 to 28**; in AP **four RRBs** merged into the **Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank (APGB)**.

## Prudential numbers

- **CRAR** minimum **9%** in India (Basel III norm 8%), plus a **2.5%** capital conservation buffer.
- **Priority-sector lending:** **40%** of adjusted net bank credit for commercial banks; **75%** for **small finance banks** and RRBs.
- **Payments banks** may hold deposits up to **₹2 lakh** per customer.
- **DICGC** insures deposits up to **₹5 lakh** per depositor per bank (since 2020).
- An **NPA** is a loan overdue for more than **90 days**; **NARCL** ("bad bank") was set up in **2021**; **MCLR (2016)** gave way to the **external benchmark (EBLR)** from **1 October 2019**.
- **FSR (June 2026):** banks' bad loans are expected to stay **below 2%** through 2028.

## 2025-26 changes

- **Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025:** depositors can name up to **four nominees** (from **1 November 2025**).
- **Urban cooperative banks** came under the BR Act in **1966**; the **2020** amendment placed them under fuller RBI supervision.
- **PMJDY** began on **28 August 2014** — the **JAM** trinity (Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, Mobile).

**Don't confuse** — *Narasimham* (1991/1998 banking reforms) with *Nachiket Mor* (2013, differentiated banks) and *P.J. Nayak* (2014, governance).

**TL;DR**
- Bank of Hindustan 1770; Imperial Bank 1921 → SBI 1 July 1955; PNB 1894; Andhra Bank 1923 Machilipatnam (Pattabhi Sitaramayya) → Union Bank 2020.
- 14 banks 19 July 1969; 6 banks 15 April 1980; 12 PSBs after 2020.
- Narasimham 1991/1998; Rajan 2008; Nachiket Mor 2013; P.J. Nayak 2014 (BBB 2016 → FSIB); Urjit Patel 2014.
- RRBs: Prathama Bank 1975, Act 1976, 50:35:15; 43 → 28 (1 May 2025); AP Grameena Bank.
- CRAR 9%; PSL 40% (SFB 75%); PB deposit ₹2 lakh; DICGC ₹5 lakh; NPA 90 days; NARCL 2021; EBLR 2019; four nominees from 1 Nov 2025.
keyPoints: The Bank of Hindustan (1770, Calcutta) was India's first bank; the General Bank of India followed in 1786.
The Presidency Banks merged into the Imperial Bank of India (1921), which became the State Bank of India on 1 July 1955.
Punjab National Bank (1894, Lahore) was the first bank wholly managed by Indians.
Andhra Bank was founded in 1923 at Machilipatnam by Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya and merged into Union Bank of India on 1 April 2020.
14 banks were nationalised on 19 July 1969 and 6 more on 15 April 1980.
Dena and Vijaya Banks merged into Bank of Baroda (1 April 2019); 10 PSBs merged into 4 on 1 April 2020, leaving 12 public sector banks.
Narasimham Committees: 1991 and 1998; Raghuram Rajan Committee on financial sector reforms: 2008.
Nachiket Mor Committee (2013) recommended payments banks and small finance banks.
P.J. Nayak Committee (2014) led to the Banks Board Bureau (2016), now FSIB (2022); Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended flexible inflation targeting.
First RRB: Prathama Bank, Moradabad, 2 October 1975; RRB Act 1976; shareholding Centre 50, sponsor bank 35, State 15.
'One State, One RRB' from 1 May 2025 cut RRBs from 43 to 28; in AP four RRBs merged into the Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank.
Minimum CRAR is 9% in India (Basel III norm 8%) plus a 2.5% capital conservation buffer.
Priority-sector lending is 40% of adjusted net bank credit for commercial banks and 75% for small finance banks.
Payments banks may hold deposits up to ₹2 lakh per customer; DICGC insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh.
A loan is an NPA when overdue for more than 90 days; NARCL (bad bank) was set up in 2021.
MCLR (2016) was replaced for new loans by the external benchmark (EBLR) from 1 October 2019.
The June 2026 FSR expects bank bad loans to stay below 2% through 2028.
Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025 lets depositors name up to four nominees from 1 November 2025.
Urban cooperative banks came under the BR Act in 1966; the 2020 amendment tightened RBI supervision.
PMJDY began on 28 August 2014 — the JAM trinity of Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and Mobile.
RRBs and Land Development Banks give direct credit to rural households; NABARD only refinances (UPSC 2013).

items.title: Money & Its Measures, Market Instruments, SEBI, Insurance and Pensions
items.body:
**In one line:** money has four functions and four RBI aggregates; short-term debt trades in the money market and shares and bonds in the capital market under SEBI; insurance and pensions have their own regulators and 2025-26 reforms.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2013/2020/2021/2023 test liquidity order, instruments and markets; current affairs test insurance FDI, UPS and UPI numbers.

## Money

- **Barter** needs a **double coincidence of wants**; money removes it.
- Four functions: **medium of exchange**, **unit of account**, **store of value**, **standard of deferred payment**.
- **Fiat money** (notes, coins — legal tender by law) vs **fiduciary money** (cheques, promissory notes — based on trust); **reserve money** = **high-powered money**.

## RBI's money aggregates

**The story**

| Aggregate | Composition |
|---|---|
| **M1** (narrow) | Currency with the public + **demand deposits** + other deposits with RBI |
| **M2** | M1 + **post office savings** deposits |
| **M3** (broad) | M1 + **time deposits** of banks |
| **M4** | M3 + all post office deposits |

- **Liquidity order (UPSC 2013):** **currency > demand deposits > savings deposits > time deposits**.
- The **money multiplier** rises with the **banking habit** of people (UPSC 2021) and falls with higher reserve ratios.
- (The source text gives US-style M2/M3 definitions with money-market funds — not the RBI's.)

## Market instruments

| Instrument | Point |
|---|---|
| **Treasury bills** | **91-, 182- and 364-day**; issued by the RBI for the Government; sold at a discount |
| **Commercial paper (CP)** | **Unsecured promissory note** issued by companies (UPSC 2020) |
| **Certificate of deposit (CD)** | Issued by banks |
| **Call money** | Overnight inter-bank lending (notice money 2-14 days) |
| **TREPS** | Replaced **CBLO** in **2018** |

- **UPSC 2023:** of government bond, call money, T-bill and stock markets, only the **government bond market** and **stock market** are **capital markets**.

## SEBI and the stock market

- **SEBI** was set up on **12 April 1988** and made statutory by the **SEBI Act, 1992**; chair **Tuhin Kanta Pandey** (since March 2025). The **Forward Markets Commission** merged with SEBI in **2015**.
- **BSE (1875)** is Asia's oldest exchange; **NSE** was set up in **1992**. **Sensex** has 30 stocks, **Nifty** 50.
- **Credit rating agencies** (CRISIL, ICRA, CARE) are regulated by **SEBI**, not the RBI.

## Insurance

- **LIC** (1956), **New India Assurance** (1919, largest general insurer); **GIC Re** is the national reinsurer; **IRDAI** (IRDA Act 1999) is headquartered at **Hyderabad**.
- **FDI cap:** **26%** → **49%** (2015) → **74%** (2021) → **100%** under a law passed in **December 2025**, with the automatic route notified in **2026**.
- Insurance penetration about **4%** against a world average of about 7% (source).

## Pensions

- **NPS** began on **1 January 2004** for new central employees; **PFRDA Act, 2013**.
- **Unified Pension Scheme (UPS)** from **1 April 2025**: **50%** of the last 12 months' average basic pay; Government contribution **18.5%**; family pension 60%.
- **Atal Pension Yojana** (2015): ₹1,000-5,000 a month.

## UPI in 2026

- **September 2026:** **24.07 billion** UPI transactions worth **₹29.37 lakh crore**, with a daily record of **802 million**.

**Don't confuse** — *CP* (companies, unsecured) with *CD* (banks); *call money* and *T-bills* (money market) with *bonds* and *stocks* (capital market).

**TL;DR**
- Barter → double coincidence; four functions; fiat vs fiduciary; reserve = high-powered money.
- M1 = C + DD + OD; M2 = M1 + PO savings; M3 = M1 + time deposits; M4 = M3 + all PO deposits; liquidity C > DD > savings > time.
- T-bills 91/182/364; CP unsecured; CD banks; TREPS replaced CBLO (2018); capital market = bonds + stocks.
- SEBI 1988/1992 (Tuhin Kanta Pandey); FMC merged 2015; BSE 1875; CRAs under SEBI.
- Insurance FDI 26 → 49 → 74 → 100%; IRDAI Hyderabad; NPS 2004; UPS 1 Apr 2025 (50%, 18.5%); UPI Sept 2026 24.07 bn.
keyPoints: Barter requires a double coincidence of wants.
Functions of money: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payment.
Fiat money is legal tender by law; fiduciary money (cheques, promissory notes) rests on trust; reserve money is high-powered money.
RBI aggregates: M1 = currency + demand deposits + other deposits with RBI; M2 = M1 + post office savings; M3 = M1 + time deposits; M4 = M3 + all post office deposits.
Liquidity order (UPSC 2013): currency > demand deposits > savings deposits > time deposits.
The money multiplier increases with the banking habit of the people (UPSC 2021).
Treasury bills are 91-, 182- and 364-day bills sold at a discount; commercial paper is an unsecured promissory note issued by companies (UPSC 2020); certificates of deposit are issued by banks.
Call money is overnight inter-bank lending; TREPS replaced CBLO in 2018.
Of government bond, call money, T-bill and stock markets, only the government bond market and stock market are capital markets (UPSC 2023).
SEBI was set up on 12 April 1988 and made statutory in 1992; Tuhin Kanta Pandey is its chairman; the Forward Markets Commission merged with SEBI in 2015.
BSE (1875) is Asia's oldest stock exchange; NSE was set up in 1992; Sensex has 30 stocks and Nifty 50.
Credit rating agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA and CARE are regulated by SEBI.
LIC dates from 1956 and New India Assurance from 1919; GIC Re is the national reinsurer; IRDAI is headquartered at Hyderabad.
Insurance FDI cap: 26% → 49% (2015) → 74% (2021) → 100% (law passed December 2025).
NPS began on 1 January 2004; PFRDA Act 2013.
Unified Pension Scheme from 1 April 2025 pays 50% of the last 12 months’ average basic pay; Government contributes 18.5%.
UPI processed 24.07 billion transactions worth ₹29.37 lakh crore in September 2026.

items.title: For Mains — RBI, Banking & Financial Markets
items.body:
## In one line

For Mains, RBI/banking is examined not as definitions but as a **policy debate**: can monetary policy and banking reform deliver price stability, resource mobilisation and inclusive growth together? (Serves Paper-4 clauses M4-1 and M4-2.)

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes | Supply-side inflation (food/fuel), legacy NPAs, slow transmission, thin credit in rural areas |
| Features | FIT framework (4% ±2% CPI), LAF corridor, MPC, SARFAESI/IBC, JAM-led inclusion |
| Significance | Anchors expectations, mobilises savings, channels credit to productive sectors |
| Impact | Lower inflation volatility; wider formal credit via UPI/Jan Dhan |
| Criticism / limits | Weak against cost-push shocks; incomplete transmission; regional credit gaps |
| Way forward | Supply-side management, faster EBLR transmission, governance reform, deeper inclusion |

## Data / committees / reports to quote

- **FIT framework** — statutory since the 2016 RBI Act amendment; **4% CPI ±2%** target.
- **Policy corridor (Oct 2026):** repo 5.50%, SDF 5.25%, MSF/Bank Rate 5.75%, CRR 3.00%, SLR 18.00%.
- **Urjit Patel Committee (2014)** recommended inflation targeting; **Nachiket Mor Committee** shaped payments/small-finance banks.
- **IBC, 2016** and **SARFAESI, 2002** for NPA resolution; **PCA** framework for weak banks.
- **PMJDY (2014)** + **UPI** (~₹314 lakh crore in FY 2025-26) for financial inclusion.

## AP angle

For an agrarian, coastal state like **Andhra Pradesh**, transmission shapes the cost of **crop loans, MSME and aquaculture credit**; **RRBs (AP Grameena Vikas Bank)**, SHG-bank linkage and Jan Dhan accounts anchor rural credit and DBT.

## Use in answers

- **Example:** cite the 2025–26 rate-cut cycle (repo cut to 5.50%) as monetary easing to support growth.
- **Quote:** monetary policy is 'a blunt instrument against supply-side inflation'.
- **Diagram idea:** draw the LAF corridor (SDF < repo < MSF) or the JAM trinity triangle.
keyPoints: Mains frames RBI/banking as a policy debate on price stability, resource mobilisation and inclusive growth (M4-1, M4-2).
Use the dimensions table: causes, features, significance, impact, criticism, way forward.
Quote FIT (2016, 4% ±2%), the Oct 2026 corridor, Urjit Patel & Nachiket Mor committees, IBC/SARFAESI, PMJDY/UPI.
Key limits: weak against supply-side inflation, incomplete transmission, regional credit gaps.
AP angle: RRBs, SHG-bank linkage and Jan Dhan underpin rural credit and DBT in AP.
